references.text: Matthew's parallel to this parable: the one who hears Jesus' words and does not do them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. The rain, the rivers, and the winds came, and the house fell, and its fall was great.
Ezekiel describes a wall built without a proper foundation, plastered with lime, which collapses when rain, hail, and storm come – a parallel to the house built without a foundation.
Proverbs say that when the storm comes, the wicked are gone, but the righteous have an eternal foundation – an image resembling the contrast between building with and without a foundation.
The wicked are overthrown and are no more, while the houses of the righteous stand firm – this mirrors the difference between the one who hears and does, and the one who hears without doing.

The preceding parable about the one who builds a house on a rock with a deep foundation forms a contrast to verse 49. Together they make up the pair of parables about hearing and doing versus hearing without doing.

James urges people to be doers of the word, not merely hearers, and warns that those who only hear deceive themselves. This is thematically parallel to the warnings in Jesus' parable about hearing without acting.
Paul emphasizes that it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law – the same principle found in Jesus' parable about the hearer who does not act.

Isaiah speaks of the cornerstone that God lays in Zion, and that justice and righteousness shall be the measuring line. Those who do not build on this foundation will experience destruction – a parallel to the house without a foundation.
